catalogTitle: תיקון פגימת הלבנה ע”י טובת עין

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the flaw of the moon, born of its jealousy, is repaired by a good eye: through the leap year's thirteenth month, through Esther becoming queen, and through Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's thirteenth year in the cave and his teaching of love between friends.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach starts from the seven 'ro'ei pnei hamelech' in the Megillah. Following the Gemara and the Chasam Sofer, their names allude to korbanos, so the angels above with the same names pleaded for the Jews. Rashi reads them as the heavenly angels busy with the leap year so that Esther would become queen. Why would angels deal with a leap year? Because the leap year repairs the flaw of the moon, which was diminished for envying the sun. Esther is the moon, and her kingship is the moon's repair. The repair is a good eye: the students of Rabbi Akiva lacked it, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a gilgul of Shimon who led the sale of Yosef, fixed it with his thirteenth year in the cave and his teaching of 'hinei mah tov'. Lag BaOmer and Purim, which fall on the same weekday, share this tikkun.

en: The seven ministers' names allude to korbanos, so the seven angels above with the same names pleaded for the Jews, as the Chasam Sofer explains.
According to Rashi, the 'knowers of the times' were the heavenly angels, who busied themselves with the leap year so that Esther would become queen and the Jews would be saved.
The leap year is a repair of the moon's flaw: the thirteenth month makes up the days by which the moon falls behind the sun.
The moon was diminished because it lacked a good eye toward the sun, and this jealousy runs through history, from the sin of the Tree of Knowledge to the sale of Yosef.
Esther is the moon, and her becoming queen is the repair of the moon's flaw.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a gilgul of Shimon who led the sale of Yosef, repaired it with a good eye and with love between friends.

title.en: Opening

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with numbers in the pesukim.

title.en: The seven ministers and the seven angels

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the seven 'ro'ei pnei hamelech' of the Megillah, whose names the Gemara connects to korbanos. The Chasam Sofer explains that what happens below happens above, so seven angels with the same names sat in judgment and pleaded for the Jews.

title.en: The 'knowers of the times' and the leap year

summary.en: On the plain level the king's advisers were experts in calculating the calendar, and a calculation about the day Vashti's father was killed is brought. Rashi reads them as the holy angels who busied themselves with the leap year so that Esther would become queen, and the Mashgiach asks what angels have to do with a leap year.

title.en: The moon's flaw and Esther as the moon

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the leap year repairs the moon, which was diminished for lacking a good eye toward the sun. This jealousy is part of creation and runs through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, Kayin and the sale of Yosef; Esther is the moon, and her becoming queen is a repair of its flaw.

title.en: The leap year of the miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that the Sages made the year of the miracle a leap year, so the angels' concern with the leap year was the moon's repair through Esther. He explains that the thirteenth month makes up the days the moon loses against the sun each year, repairing a flaw that came from jealousy and a narrow eye.

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai repairs with a good eye

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the students of Rabbi Akiva, who did not honor one another, with the thirteenth middah of Tomer Devorah, seeing another's good. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a gilgul of Shimon who led the sale of Yosef, repaired it with a good eye and love of friends, and like Yosef's twelve years plus one, his twelve years in the cave became thirteen.

title.en: Lag BaOmer and Purim, and the task of the generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Lag BaOmer always falls on the weekday of Purim and explains that they are a pair: Purim's gathering of all the Jews and Rabbi Shimon's 'sheves achim gam yachad' both repair the sale of Yosef and the moon. He closes that the task of this generation is the middah of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, love and peace between friends.

catalogTitle: A Day in which Sublime עולמות are Revealed

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Purim a sublime world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of all Jewish souls where no accuser can reach, is revealed, so that Hashem's unconditional love reaches even the most forgotten Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying Purim is misunderstood: Chazal and the Chasam Sofer place it above Pesach and Shavuos. Following the Noam Elimelech, he describes a world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of the souls, where the trace of holiness in every Jew can never be erased. The Jews at the 'end of the Sefer Torah', whom Moshe Rabbeinu forgot and Amalek and Haman thought were forgotten, are remembered there by Hashem. That world is revealed on Purim. The Megillah reveals Hashem's hidden love: He loves the generation of concealment most, like a king who visits his bride even in a tannery. Purim, like Yom Kippur, is decided by a lottery, the expression of a will beyond reason, and carries the holiness of Keser. The Megillah is a personal letter, unrolled without fear of accusers. Finally, Purim, like Yom Kippur, depends on the unity of all Jews, which is why Shushan keeps Purim with Yerushalayim.

en: The Mashgiach says Purim is not a day of frivolity; it is higher than every other day of the Jewish calendar, even Pesach and Shavuos.
There is a world called 'Kol Yisrael', the root of the Jewish souls, where no Jew is rejected and the Satan has no access, and it is revealed on Purim.
The Megillah reveals Hashem's love in a time of concealment: Hashem loves the generation of hastarah more than all others, even when it cannot see Him.
Purim and Yom Kippur are both decided by a lottery, which expresses Hashem's will that has no reason, and both draw from the level of Keser.
The Megillah is called an iggeres, a letter Hashem addresses personally to each Jew, especially those weak in Yiddishkeit.
Like Yom Kippur, Purim comes from the unity of all Jews, which is why Shushan, where the Jews gathered together, keeps Purim on the day Yerushalayim does.

title.en: Purim is higher than every other day

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying Purim is misunderstood as a day of frivolity, and brings the Chasam Sofer that it is greater than Pesach and Shavuos, and the Rambam that the Megillah will remain when other festivals are nullified. He then introduces, from the Noam Elimelech, a world called 'Kol Yisrael', connected to the Mishnah's 'all of Israel has a share'.

title.en: No Jew is lost at the root of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the question what becomes of a sinner, answered by Hashem with teshuvah, and explains that in the deepest level of Torah no Jew is rejected and the trace of holiness is never erased. He describes the Avos as the trunk of the tree and the point of Yaakov in every Jew, and the 'forgotten' Jews at the end of the Sefer Torah, whom Moshe Rabbeinu forgot like the hooks of the pillars.

title.en: Amalek's mistake and the hidden bond

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek and Haman attacked the Jews on the fringes, thinking they were forgotten, but in the world of 'Kol Yisrael', revealed on Purim, every Jew is remembered and the Satan cannot reach. He discusses Achashverosh's feast celebrating that the Beis HaMikdash would not be rebuilt, and the Gemara's opening verse that Hashem never despises His people, and a Midrash reading Achashverosh as Hashem.

title.en: Megillas Esther reveals the concealment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the world of Purim never opened, not even on Pesach or Shavuos, until the Megillah, which reveals the hastarah (concealment) alluded to in 'haster astir'. He describes today's confusing concealment, how the Megillah is understood only at its end, and a sefer's teaching that one should tremble at the blessing 'al mikra Megillah', which calls down that world.

title.en: The King loves the generation of concealment

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'the king loved Esther more than all the women' as Hashem's love for the generation of concealment, which thought it was forgotten. He explains the hidden vav of 'kalaso' as the hidden Groom, and the Zohar's parable of the king who visits his bride in a tannery: the Megillah tells that Hashem is bound to His people in every state.

title.en: Purim, Yom Kippur and the lottery

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'Yom Kippurim, a day like Purim': on both days the main thing is a lottery. From the two identical goats of Yom Kippur and Rav Tzadok's teaching, he explains that Yaakov may look like Esav but Hashem knows he is His, and that a lottery, like a will that has no reason, shows Hashem's choice of His people is beyond explanation.

title.en: The crown of Keser and the personal letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Kedushah of Keser said at Musaf on Shabbos and all day on Yom Kippur, and that, per the Arizal, a Jew has this holiness the whole day of Purim; he touches on the threefold Purim in Yerushalayim that year. He then explains why the Megillah is called an iggeres: a letter addressed personally to each Jew, like a letter to grandparents, sent especially to the weak, and he likens Purim to the crown on the yud.

title.en: Above the Name: an uncovered Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'lifnei Hashem tit'haru' as a level above the Name Havayah, and that the Megillah, which lacks Hashem's Name, is wholly above it, like a person who is more than his name. He contrasts holy objects that are kept covered for fear of the Satan, such as matzah, the Sefer Torah and the shofar, with the Megillah, which is unfolded entirely because on Purim there is no accuser.

title.en: The unity of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the essence of Purim, like Yom Kippur, is the world of 'Kol Yisrael' where all souls merge into one; Yom Kippur does not atone for one who is at odds with another Jew. Haman's accusation was that the Jews were scattered and divided, and Esther answered by gathering them together; he connects this to Yerushalayim, which joins all Jews together.

title.en: Shushan like Yerushalayim; blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Purim's single shared feast and mishloach manos to an eruv uniting all Jews, and says Shushan merited to keep Purim with Yerushalayim because of that unity. He closes with blessings for a joyous Purim, notes a sefer that a year when Purim falls on Friday is a sign for the geulah, and mentions his plan to travel to Eretz Yisrael for the threefold Purim.

catalogTitle: רשב”י מגלה שיש חן מיוחד בכל יחיד מישראל

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew, even the lowest, has a hidden virtue and grace before Hashem that no other Jew has, and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the revealer of secrets, revealed this hidden preciousness of every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rav Tzadok HaKohen's teaching that every Jew has a unique grace before Hashem and a virtue no other Jew has, which makes him a king; this is why Rabbi Shimon says all Jews are sons of kings. The virtue is hidden, like the sod level of the Torah, and Rabbi Shimon, who reveals secrets, reveals it. The students of Rabbi Akiva died for not honoring one another, failing to see this hidden virtue; on Lag Ba'omer it shines more than on other days. He links the four levels of Torah to the four elements, with earth as the lowest Jew, and shows from the shemitah of the land and the Torah's care for the animals that holiness reaches even there. He closes with the Zohar's account of Rabbi Shimon's passing, the name formed from Kiddush, and Rabbi Shimon's special help for the last generation before Moshiach.

en: Every Jew has a special grace before Hashem and a virtue that no other Jew has, and through it he is a king over all Jews.
This virtue is hidden, like the sod level of the Torah, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who reveals secrets, reveals the preciousness of every Jew.

The students of Rabbi Akiva did not honor one another because they did not appreciate the hidden virtue of the other; on Lag Ba'omer the preciousness of each Jew shines out more than on any other day.

The four levels of Torah correspond to the four elements; earth is the lowest level, and the shemitah of the land shows that the holiness of Shabbos reaches down even to it, that is, to the lowest Jew.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is the aspect of Shabbos, and his main concern is the last generation, the generation of the footsteps of Moshiach, whom he helps to be raised to the greatest levels.

title.en: Every Jew has a hidden grace

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Tzadok HaKohen that every Jew has a unique grace and virtue that makes him a king, the reason Rabbi Shimon says all Jews are sons of kings. The virtue is hidden like the sod of the Torah, and Rabbi Shimon, revealer of secrets, reveals it.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva's students and the lowest element

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rabbi Akiva's students died for not honoring each other's hidden virtue, and that Lag Ba'omer reveals it. He sets the four levels of Torah against the four elements, with earth as the lowest Jew, and says even earth has a Shabbos and every Jew has a portion in Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Shabbos reaches down to the earth

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the holiness of Shabbos reaches down to the lowest Jew, brings the Beis Aharon that as Hashem is blessed for all so Rabbi Shimon is for all, and connects Lag Ba'omer with parshas Behar and the shemitah of the land, the amei ha'aretz, and the Zohar's teaching that Rabbi Shimon is the aspect of Shabbos.

title.en: Shemitah, the animals, and 'afra afra'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in shemitah the Torah provides even for the animals, an allusion to Jews who seem to have lost their tzelem Elokim, so Lag Ba'omer is a yom tov for the lowly. He ties this to the tribe of Dan, the last camp, and to the students of Rabbi Akiva, and brings the Zohar on Rabbi Shimon's passing, that the earth must not be proud, since he is not consumed by it.

title.en: The name from Kiddush and the last generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls this a comfort for Jews: the holiness of the name formed from the initials of yichud, brachah and kedushah in the Kiddush of Shabbos reaches down to 'the animals and the beasts'. He repeats the Beis Aharon and concludes that Rabbi Shimon's main concern is our generation before Moshiach, ending with a tefilah.

catalogTitle: שיהיו דברי תורה חדשים עליך; ביאתם לסיני בתשובה

oneLiner.en: On Rosh Chodesh Sivan the Mashgiach teaches that the Torah is given anew every year, and that the arrival at Sinai, made in unity and teshuvah, is a time to take on new resolutions whose acceptance itself sustains the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by explaining why the people gather in the days before Shavuos: sitting together as one man with one heart is a goal in itself, and the Gemara shows that avodah needs a stir of many people. Following the Avodas Yisroel, he studies the verses of Bachodesh hashlishi day by day. Rashi's words 'that the words of Torah be new to you as if given today' answer the Magen Avraham's question about 'the day of the giving of our Torah': it is given anew each year. Rosh Chodesh is the renewal of the moon, a time to take on new kabbalos, and from the Simchas HaRegel and the Gemara in Shabbos he shows how precious acceptance itself is. Leaving Rephidim means shaking off weakness in Torah with teshuvah. He speaks of unity, facing the 'east', the dangers facing Jews and the apathy of the world, and ends that each Jew's added acceptance can tip the whole world.

en: Sitting together as one man with one heart before Shavuos is a goal in itself, and it is also the setting for words of chizuk.
The Torah is given anew every Shavuos, so the words of Torah must feel new each day, as if given today.
Rosh Chodesh, the renewal of the moon, renews the spiritual growth in a Jew's soul and is a time to take on new kabbalos.
Accepting the mitzvos is itself precious to Hashem; the world waited not for the giving of the Torah but for the Jews' acceptance of it.
Leaving Rephidim, read as weakness in Torah, means shaking off that weakness with teshuvah and strengthening oneself in Torah.
A Jew should face 'east', toward the one point of glorifying Hashem and toward the future, not back at lost days.
Since the world's existence hangs on accepting the Torah, each Jew's added acceptance before Shavuos can tip the whole world to merit.

title.en: Why gather before Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sitting together as one man with one heart is a goal in itself, brings the Avodas Yisroel's custom of learning the verses of Bachodesh hashlishi each day from Rosh Chodesh, and cites the Gemara that the Temple service was arranged with several lotteries so there would be a stir of people.

title.en: Torah new each day; Rosh Chodesh renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the Magen Avraham's question on 'the day of the giving of our Torah' by explaining that the Torah is given anew every year, reads Rashi's 'that the words of Torah be new to you', and explains that the Jews arrived at Sinai on Rosh Chodesh because the renewal of the moon renews a Jew's soul and is the time for new kabbalos, even though all beginnings are hard.

title.en: The power of kabbalah

summary.en: From the Simchas HaRegel, citing Rabbi Gedalia Chayun on a Midrash, the Mashgiach explains that every mitzvah a convert does is compounded by the mitzvah of her acceptance; the Gemara's 'you captured My heart with one of your eyes' shows that acceptance alone is dear to Hashem, and the world waited for the Jews' acceptance of the Torah.

title.en: Leaving Rephidim with teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Rosh Chodesh is when the Jews accepted upon themselves with teshuvah, urges taking on one middah to work on, reads Rephidim as weakness in Torah, and brings Rashi that their arrival at Sinai and their departure from Rephidim were both with teshuvah.

title.en: One heart, facing east

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Sinai's unity with the strife elsewhere, ties Sivan's sign of twins to unity, and explains Rashi's 'wherever it says neged, it means facing east' as being turned toward the one point of glorifying Hashem and toward the future; he ends with the Gemara that the earth feared until the Jews accepted the Torah.

title.en: The danger and the world's apathy

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the danger facing Jews in Eretz Yisroel and the growing hatred elsewhere, says the world suffers from apathy and distraction, and tells how his father-in-law once rebuked a Vienna community meeting busy with honor while Hitler grew strong; the only counsel is accepting Torah and mitzvos and davening for Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Each Jew can tip the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the world's existence hung on the acceptance of the Torah, brings the Gemara that one person can tip the whole world to merit, asks each one to take on a little more learning and coming earlier to davening, and closes with Rashi that Moshe's ascents were early in the morning, a blessing and a l'chaim.

catalogTitle: ויחן שם ישראל - חשיבות דיבוק חברים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Rosh Chodesh Sivan the Jews camped before Sinai 'as one man with one heart', and that this unity among friends is the general principle of the Torah and the preparation for receiving it; in the second part he explains why Shavuos, the fiftieth day, stands above time and counting.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'bachodesh hashlishi... bayom hazeh' and Rashi's reading that it was Rosh Chodesh, a new beginning tied to Matan Torah. Rashi compares leaving Refidim to arriving at Sinai, both in teshuvah. The Mashgiach explains that Refidim was a place of separation, which let Amalek in, and the repair was 'vayichan', camping as one man with one heart. This is why the Haggadah praises nearing Sinai even without the Torah: love of one's fellow is the klal of the Torah, and on that day nothing was said, yet they became one. He brings the Kobriner and the Lechovitcher and urges friends to sit together. He then asks why Shavuos is the day of the giving of the Torah and explains that the fiftieth day is above counting, like the Levi'im, Aharon and Moshe Rabbeinu, and that Moshe, the 'shofar' of Klal Yisrael, brings the festivals each year.

en: Rosh Chodesh Sivan, when the Jews camped before Sinai as one man with one heart, is a day whose whole theme is unity among Jews.
Refidim was a place of separation among Jews, which gave Amalek his power; the teshuvah on leaving it was their unity.
Coming close to Sinai in unity is the general principle of the Torah, 'love your fellow as yourself', while the giving of the Torah brought its details.
In a lowly generation little is demanded, and a small effort toward unity among friends is precious in heaven and can bring great things.
The fiftieth day is above counting and above time, which is why it is not counted, like the Levi'im, Aharon and Moshe Rabbeinu who stand above number.
Moshe Rabbeinu, the 'shofar' of Klal Yisrael, could rule over time, and he brings the power of Matan Torah to every Jewish shul each Shavuos.

title.en: Opening

summary.en: About three minutes at the start.

title.en: Rosh Chodesh Sivan and leaving Refidim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'bachodesh hashlishi... bayom hazeh' with Rashi that it was Rosh Chodesh, and explains that a new month, a new beginning, is tied to Matan Torah. He then brings Rashi that their leaving Refidim was compared to their arrival at Sinai: both in teshuvah.

title.en: 'Vayichan': as one man with one heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi on 'vayichan sham Yisrael', that they camped as one man with one heart, and explains that Refidim was a place of separation that let Amalek in, so their teshuvah was unity. He adds that two Jews together form Hashem's Name, and that today's theme is that Jews should sit together and love one another.

title.en: Nearing Sinai: the klal of the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what virtue there is in coming close to Sinai without receiving the Torah, as the Haggadah says, and answers that the unity of that day is 'love your fellow as yourself', Rabbi Akiva's great principle of the Torah. He brings the practice of sitting together in friendship from Beis Aharon and the Gemara that on Rosh Chodesh nothing was said to them.

title.en: One family; naaseh v'nishma as one

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rav Moshe of Kobrin that when Jews sit together as one family they are not excluded from the klal, and explains that naaseh v'nishma was so great because it was said as one. He contrasts the decline of the generations with the greater virtue of today, when little is demanded and a small effort can merit great things.

title.en: Greater light in the darkness; no complaints against friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because the darkness is greater, Hashem lights greater lamps, as seen in the revelations from Rashbi, the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov, and the small piece one can give is precious in heaven. He brings the Lechovitcher that a punishment is to be sent complaints against one's Rebbe and then against one's friends, and says one must bear a friend's faults, since every Jew is a part of G-d above, as the preparation for receiving the Torah.

title.en: Interlude

summary.en: An interlude of almost fourteen minutes.

title.en: Why Shavuos is 'the time of the giving of the Torah'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the question that the Torah was given on the fifty-first day of the Omer, on Shabbos, so how is Shavuos called the day of the giving of the Torah, and the Chok Yaakov's discussion of it. He brings that whenever the parsha of Matan Torah is read, it is as if one stands before Sinai receiving the Torah.

title.en: The fiftieth day and the uncounted Levi'im

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi on the dots over Aharon's name in the count of the Levi'im, and the Chok Yaakov that Shavuos depends on the fiftieth day of the count, not the date. The fiftieth day is above place, time and number, where 'one' is not the smallest number but the only one, like the Levi'im who were not counted with the camps because they stand above counting.

title.en: Three levels of one miracle

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Mishnah of ten miracles in the Beis Hamikdash does not count that the place of the Aron took no space, and answers that in the Kodesh HaKodashim heaven's nature rules, so it is no miracle, like fish in the sea. Bowing with room in the Azarah was a visible miracle on Yom Tov, and finding lodging in Yerushalayim a hidden one: the same miracle at three levels.

title.en: Aharon, Moshe and the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that among the uncounted there are levels: the Levi'im, then Aharon, of whom not even the firstborn part was counted, and Moshe Rabbeinu, the fiftieth gate, connected with Rabbi Akiva's 'great principle'. He brings that the Torah is above time, the dispute whether it was given on the sixth or seventh of Sivan, and that the sixth of Sivan was set from creation.

title.en: Moshe Rabbeinu, the shofar who brings the festivals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Moshe Rabbeinu, the shofar of Klal Yisrael, stood above time and added a day, as later the heads of Beis Din could set the months, while today the calendar is fixed on the sixth of Sivan. 'Vayedaber Moshe es mo'adei Hashem' means Moshe brings the festivals to the Jews, so every Shavuos he comes to every shul where the parsha is read, and it is truly 'bayom hazeh'.

title.en: Counting the last sefirah together

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last count of sefirah includes all the days, speaks of 'sur mera va'aseh tov' as the work of sefirah, and asks that everyone come together to daven and count sefirah together.

catalogTitle: The Message of the "אגרת הפורים": Hashem is Near to You!

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that on Purim heaven comes down to earth, so the Megillah is a personal letter from Hashem to every Jew, and its mitzvos, above all tzedakah and the seudah, open doors that stay closed the rest of the year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying Purim is beyond understanding, as the Gemara's 'ad d'lo yada' hints. Following the Maharal, he explains the haste in the Megillah: the miracle comes from heaven, where there is no time, and pushes time aside. Purim is therefore like Shabbos, a taste of the world to come, and Klal Yisrael accepted the Torah then with love. He describes three days of preparation before Purim and the idea that Hashem is a person's shadow. He shows hidden names of Hashem in the Megillah, spelled for din or for chesed, then explains why the Megillah is called an iggeres: a personal letter, sweet only to the one it is addressed to. The four mitzvos of Purim correspond to the four letters of Hashem's name; tzedakah on Purim lights up far higher worlds. He ends with the joy of the seudah as a day of reconciliation, and two stories showing what Purim accomplishes.

en: The miracle of Purim comes from heaven, where there is no time, so on its way down it pushes time aside; this is why everything in the Megillah happens in a hurry.
On Purim heaven comes down to earth; it is a taste of the eternal Shabbos, which is why Shabbos clothes are worn on Purim though it is a weekday.
The Megillah is called an iggeres because it is a personal letter: sweet and meaningful only to one who has a bond with Hashem.
The four mitzvos of Purim correspond to the four letters of Hashem's name, which Amalek keeps from being complete.
Tzedakah on Purim is like pressing the master switch: the same act lights up far higher worlds than tzedakah during the year.
Just as on Purim tzedakah is given to whoever stretches out a hand, Hashem gives on Purim to whoever turns to Him, even the undeserving.
The Purim seudah is a feast of reconciliation with Hashem, like Yom Kippur, and should be eaten alert and aware of its purpose.

title.en: Purim above time: heaven comes down

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'ad d'lo yada' and, following the Maharal, explains why everything in the Megillah happens in haste: the miracle comes from heaven, where there is no time. On Purim heaven comes down to earth, a preview of the eternal Shabbos.

title.en: Shabbos clothes and three days of preparation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Shabbos clothes are worn on Purim, brings that the Torah was accepted with love on Purim and the Chasam Sofer on the light of the Megillah, and describes the days before Purim as days of preparation. Since Hashem is a person's shadow, one prepares with kedushah to receive His gifts.

title.en: Hidden names of Hashem in the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows three places where Hashem's name is hidden in the first or last letters of words: Haman draws down din with letters spelled backwards at word ends, Esther answers with chesed in letters spelled straight at word beginnings, and in Haman's downfall din comes mixed with chesed.

title.en: The Megillah as a personal letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings an explanation from a talmid of the Ba'al Shem Tov of why the Megillah is called an iggeres, with the parable of a family letter full of small talk that is precious to the parents and meaningless to a stranger. So the Megillah is sweet to one bound to Hashem, and every word should be heard.

title.en: Four mitzvos and the four letters of Hashem's name

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Amalek keeps Hashem's name incomplete and that the four mitzvos of Purim correspond to its four letters; completing them perfectly would bring the geulah. He urges learning the Megillah beforehand from holy sources and preparing much money for tzedakah.

title.en: Tzedakah on Purim: the master switch

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tzedakah forms Hashem's name through the coin, the hand, the arm and the receiver, and that on Purim it carries an added mitzvah. With a parable of two identical switches, one lighting a room and one a whole tower, he shows that Purim tzedakah reaches far higher worlds.

title.en: The seudah: reconciliation like Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the joy of the seudah through 'kimu v'kiblu': Purim is like Yom Kippur, a day of making up with Hashem, as in the old Purim song about reconciling. The sins that insulate a person from Hashem are removed, and every word of the Megillah creates a malach.

title.en: Whoever stretches out a hand: doors open on Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim tzedakah is given without checking who asks, and so Hashem gives on Purim to whoever turns to Him in emunah. Purim opens doors closed all year, as the Gemara's opening 'pischa' and Mordechai's name Pesachyah hint, and even neshamos are helped then.

title.en: The Spinka Rebbe and the heavenly chamber

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Spinka Rebbe's story of a young man who read the Megillah on the second night of Pesach, and a neshamah that came to ask him to rule whether this made it Purim, so that a heavenly chamber open only on Purim would let it in. He concludes that Purim can do what even the Seder cannot.

title.en: A seudah by day, and the dike of Amsterdam

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Gemara that a Purim seudah eaten at night does not count as a call to eat it with the brightness of day, and tells how Rabbi Lazar of Amsterdam saved the city from a leaking dike by feasting on Purim. He closes with the importance of hearing Parshas Zachor on the coming Shabbos.

catalogTitle: כל יהודי הוא מיוחס - בן להקב”ה. נפלאותך ומחשבותיך אלינו - לבל ידח ממנו נדח

oneLiner.en: On Yom HaMeyuchas the Mashgiach teaches that every Jew is a meyuchas, a son of the King, and that Hashem's thoughts are all directed at bringing every Jewish soul, even the most distant, to its tikkun, as seen in the line of David and in Menashe's halachah of where to cut the bread.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens on Yom HaMeyuchas, the second of Sivan: the yetzer hara's greatest trick is making a Jew forget he is a king's son. Through the pesukim of the day he shows how Hashem first lifted the Jews to Yerushalayim for the Korban Pesach and then returned them, because a king's son must earn what is his by right. He reads 've'ata' as a call to do teshuvah now rather than wait for another gilgul. From 'nifle'osecha u'machshevosecha eleinu' he explains that every soul is a letter in Hashem's Sefer Torah, so none may be lost; the hidden, puzzling paths of Beis David, through Tamar, Ruth and yibum, are part of this plan. Boaz's hint that Menashe would come from Ruth leads to the Gemara of Rav Ashi learning from Menashe where to break bread. Stories of Belz show that a brachah repairs souls in food, and the crust baked first is Hashem's sign of which piece reaches its tikkun first.

en: The Mashgiach says the yetzer hara's greatest scheme is to make a Jew forget that he is a king's son, a meyuchas, with virtues he did not earn himself.
Hashem showed the Jews their destination by bringing them to Yerushalayim for the Korban Pesach, but brought them back because a king's son must work through the process himself.
'Ve'ata' means now: the Mashgiach asks why wait for a later time or another gilgul to do teshuvah and accept the Torah.
All of Hashem's thoughts are concentrated on the Jewish people's tikkun; every soul is a letter in His Sefer Torah, so a soul that has not completed itself must return until it does.
Malchus Beis David comes into the world through hidden and puzzling paths, such as Tamar, Ruth and yibum, because it is built from the tikkun of souls that were pushed away.
Menashe, whom Boaz called the 'vinegar' that would come from Ruth, became the teacher of all Israel through the halachah of where to break bread.
Food holds sparks and souls awaiting their tikkun, and a brachah said with kavanah repairs them.

title.en: Every Jew a meyuchas, a king's son

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that on this day every Jew should feel he is a meyuchas, and that the yetzer hara's chief trick is making him forget he is a king's son. He brings the Avodas Yisrael's custom of learning the pesukim of each day from Rosh Chodesh Sivan, Rashi's comparison of the departure from Refidim to the arrival at Sinai, and the pesukim of the second of Sivan.

title.en: Brought to Yerushalayim and brought back

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the words Hashem spoke to Moshe on this day are said again every year and the soul hears them. On 'va'avi eschem elai' he brings Targum Yonasan that the Jews were carried to Yerushalayim for the Korban Pesach and returned, and asks why; he answers that a Jew has his destination in potential but must reach it in actual through his own work, like a king's son.

title.en: Onkelos, Ramban and 've'ata'

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Onkelos, who renders 'elai' as being brought near to Hashem's service out of respect, with the Ramban, who reads it as Hashem dwelling together with the Jews like a father with a child. He then reads 've'ata' as a call to do teshuvah now, and begins explaining 'segulah' as a hidden treasure.

title.en: A hidden treasure and 'na'aseh' every year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Jews' virtues are hidden like a king's treasure that only Hashem understands, bringing a Rebbe's reading of Haman's words. He describes how the people answered together without waiting for the elders, and says the Torah is eternal, so every year on this day every Jewish soul again cries out 'kol asher diber Hashem na'aseh'.

title.en: Why wait for another gilgul?

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to 've'ata' and brings a parable from Lechovitch about a man who keeps returning to the world only to act foolishly again. From 'nifle'osecha u'machshevosecha eleinu' he explains that all of Hashem's thoughts are directed at the tikkun of the Jews, and that a soul missing a mitzvah must return in another gilgul to complete itself, since Hashem's Torah is whole.

title.en: Every soul a letter; Naomi gathers the sparks

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jewish soul is part of one of the letters of the Torah, so a missing soul would invalidate the Sefer Torah. He turns to Megillas Rus: Elimelech went to Moav, where sparks of kedushah were hidden from which David and Moshiach must come, and Naomi, representing the Shechinah, went along to gather them. He connects this to the Rambam's sign of Moshiach, gathering the dispersed of Israel.

title.en: Beis David built through yibum

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Shavuos is the time of gathering, when the Jews camped 'as one man with one heart', and that Moshiach is Hashem's instrument to gather and repair all Jews. He shows that Malchus Beis David repeatedly came through yibum, with Yehudah and Tamar and with Boaz and Ruth, because yibum is the tikkun of a soul that was pushed away.

title.en: Boaz's hint: Menashe the 'vinegar'

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Chazal that Boaz's words to Ruth about dipping her bread in vinegar hinted that Menashe, whose deeds were sour, would descend from her. He describes Menashe, son of the tzaddik Chizkiyahu, who placed an idol in the Heichal, and the dispute whether he has a share in the World to Come, and introduces the Gemara of Rav Ashi.

title.en: Menashe teaches Rav Ashi where to cut

summary.en: The Mashgiach retells the Gemara in Sanhedrin: Menashe came to Rav Ashi in a dream and taught him to break bread from the place baked first, and this halachah is codified for all generations. So every Jew who says hamotzi follows Menashe, his rebbe; Boaz was in fact comforting Ruth, and the Mashgiach asks why this halachah specifically came through Menashe, noting that a person's Torah is his very soul.

title.en: The kugel on the floor and the glass of brandy

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells that at Reb Sholom of Belz's tish a piece of kugel fell to the floor and he had it picked up and eaten, and explains that eating is not a mere biological function: souls and sparks in food are rectified by a proper brachah. He tells of a Jew who drank brandy without a brachah, and a tzaddik who revealed that his father's soul had been in the drink awaiting its tikkun.

title.en: The prayers of a wheat kernel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Reb Sholom of Belz's explanation: a kernel of wheat prayed at every stage, growing, harvest, grinding, baking, to reach its tikkun, until it became challah and then Shabbos kugel at the tzaddik's tish; letting it fall would waste all those prayers. The Mashgiach concludes that a Jew should eat with thought and make a brachah with kavanah, and that this repairs the souls hidden in the food.

title.en: The melachos of bread and the crust baked first

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the melachos of bread in the Gemara Shabbos are stages of the tikkun that came after Adam's sin, ending with baking. He asks why Rav Ashi did not know where to break bread and why not from the tastiest part, and answers that the place baked first is a sign of Hashem's plan that this piece reach its tikkun first; one must look into Hashem's intention in all of Torah and mitzvos.

title.en: Hashem's intention, and Menashe's teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts selling chametz, which serves Hashem's intention that a Jew not own chametz, with selling Eretz Yisrael for Shemitah, which goes against it. Returning to the bread, he says Beis David is a seed meant to repair the world, and retells the Gemara of Menashe's teshuvah, which Hashem accepted out of chesed against the angels' claims; Menashe is a sample of the wondrous ways of David's line, which is why his soul brought the halachah of hamotzi.

catalogTitle: ביאור עמוק על מגילת רות. השכינה - נעמי' באה אל מואב להוציא משם ניצוץ משיח - זה רות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Megillas Rus as the story of how the spark of Moshiach is drawn out of Moav in a time like ikvesa d'Meshicha, and how Rus, who held to the old tradition and accepted the Torah when it was hard, is the model for accepting the Torah on Shavuos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that Rus is so named because David, who came from her, sated Hashem with songs even in hard times. He brings the Gemara that Machlon and Kilyon despaired of the redemption, and the mekubalim's teaching on gilgulim, and explains that the Shechinah, Naomi, went down to Moav to draw out the holy soul of Rus. He then asks why the megillah opens with the days when the judges were judged, and why Chazal read immodesty into its verses. Through the Gemara's signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha, he explains that before Moshiach the lower forces of evil must be kept busy, like Iyov at the Sea, so chutzpah and disorder accompany the birth of Moshiach. Rus, who converted in hard times and clung to her mother-in-law's way, brought Moshiach. He closes with Malachi, Shavuos, and a call to prepare for kabbalas haTorah.

en: Rus is named for David, who came from her and could sing to Hashem even on a day of trouble, knowing that hard times are also from Hashem and good times will return.
Naomi represents the Shechinah, who went down into Moav, the territory of the sitra achra, to draw out the spark of Moshiach, Rus, and this is why there had to be a famine and Elimelech had to leave.
Before Moshiach, the lower forces of evil, which oppose Hashem's plan, must be kept busy with something, like a bone thrown to a dog, and this is the source of the chaos of ikvesa d'Meshicha.
The megillah opens with the generation that judged its judges because the signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha, chutzpah, famine and immodesty, accompany the birth of the spark of David and Moshiach.
Rus converted when it was hard to be a Jew, giving up royalty, and her reward was to live to see Shlomo's kingship, a time when converts are not accepted.
The disorder of the generation does not bring Moshiach; it is only a symptom. Rus brought Moshiach by holding to her mother-in-law's old way, the opposite of Orpah who turned her back.
Shavuos, when the Torah is received, is a time of power to leave the exile, and the Mashgiach calls for preparing for kabbalas haTorah in the remaining days.

title.en: Why she is called Rus

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Rus is named for David, who sated Hashem with songs. He explains that Rus accepted poverty and disgrace for the Torah, and that David could sing even on a day of trouble because he knew hard times are also from Hashem.

title.en: Gilgulim, Shavuos and the Shechinah in Moav

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Machlon and Kilyon despaired of the redemption, and the mekubalim's teaching that the people of the megillah were gilgulim come to rectify earlier deeds. He explains that the Torah must be kept whole, so a soul returns to complete it, and that the Shechinah, Naomi, went down to Moav to draw out the holy soul of Rus.

title.en: The generation that judged its judges

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the chaos of the days when the judges were judged and asks: the opening words of a megillah usually set its background, yet Megillas Rus says nothing further about this situation, speaking only of Rus, Boaz and David's lineage.

title.en: Chazal read immodesty into the megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Chazal that Boaz slept at the edge of the grain pile to guard it from being used for immorality, and that he asked about Rus because she did not behave like the other girls with the reapers. He contrasts this with the Gemara where Rabbi Yochanan refuses to suspect the maidens who spoke at length to Shaul, and asks why Chazal here read immodesty into the verses.

title.en: The signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the Gemara's description of the time before Moshiach: chutzpah, hunger, scorn for Torah scholars and the fearful of sin, the young shaming the old, and nothing to lean on but our Father in Heaven. He explains the erev rav as those who act for themselves and not for Heaven, and asks why the world must break down before Moshiach instead of improving step by step.

title.en: Keeping the lower forces of evil busy

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the forces of evil have layers: the higher ones know Hashem and do His will, but the lowest do not want His plan fulfilled. He brings the Midrash that at Kerias Yam Suf the Satan accused Yisrael and Hashem sent him to Iyov, and concludes that before Moshiach Hashem gives the Satan something to occupy him, like a bone thrown to a dog so it will not disturb the feast.

title.en: The megillah's goal is David and Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the whole purpose of Megillas Rus is its last verse, the birth of David, so its theme is the coming of Moshiach. When the Shechinah goes into Moav to rescue the spark of David and Moshiach, the sitra achra must be given something, and so the time of the Judges bears the signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha, including the hunger and Elimelech's refusal to give charity.

title.en: Chutzpah as the camouflage of Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his question: since the megillah does not state the signs openly, Chazal find them by remez and derash in Boaz's lying at the edge of the pile and in the girls with the reapers. Generations later, in David's time, there was no such immodesty, so Rabbi Yochanan would not suspect the maidens. The very first point of Moshiach, through Lot's daughter who named her son Moav, also began with chutzpah, which covers the coming of Moshiach and keeps the forces of evil busy.

title.en: Rus's complete reward and 'stay the night'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Boaz's blessing that Rus's reward will be complete: the Gemara says converts are not accepted in the days of Moshiach or Shlomo, and the Rambam explains that a convert is accepted when being a Jew is hard. Rus gave up royalty to convert in hard times, so her reward was to see Shlomo's glory. He then brings Chazal on 'stay the night': through the night of exile, if good people do not redeem, Hashem Himself will.

title.en: From Malachi to Rus

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Rus begins right after Malachi, the last prophet, who closes with 'remember the Torah of Moshe' and the promise of Eliyahu, who will turn the hearts of fathers to sons. Until Eliyahu comes, the generations are torn apart, which is the state of 'the days when the judges were judged'; this is a sign Moshiach is coming, a reason to hope and not to despair like Machlon and Kilyon.

title.en: How Rus brought Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects Rus to Shavuos, when David was born and when, according to the Zohar, there is power to leave the exile through the Torah. The immodest of that generation were only symptoms of Moshiach, like a swallow before spring; Rus, unlike Orpah, held to her mother-in-law's old ways and so brought Moshiach. He says every Jew must learn from her to accept the Torah even when the whole world is against it, like Avraham ha'Ivri, and that the Torah was given in the desert.

title.en: 'And now': preparing for kabbalas haTorah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'and now, if you will listen' with Rashi that all beginnings are hard: now it is hard, but later it will be sweet, and those who held out in exile like Rus will see the kingdom. He brings the Gemara that with Torah a full vessel holds more, and calls for using the remaining days of hagbalah to prepare and take on kabbalos for kabbalas haTorah.

catalogTitle: פורים Reveals the Essence of the אידישע נשמה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Purim reveals the innermost root of every Jewish soul, where even the lowest Jew wants Hashem's will and remains beloved, which is why Purim stands higher than Yom Kippur.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by rejecting the view of Purim as a carnival and cites the Chasam Sofer and Rav Tzadok HaKohen that its holiness surpasses even Yom Kippur. Since each sedra shapes its week, illustrated by stories of the Rebbe of Belz and of the Ba'al HaTanya with the Maggid, he turns to the lechem hapanim in the first sedra of Adar. With the Noam Elimelech he describes Knesses Yisrael, the root where all souls are one and no sin reaches. The Rambam's explanation of coerced consent shows that every Jew inwardly wants Hashem's will; this root, 'reishis', is above letters and thought. Yom Kippur reaches it after ten days, Purim reveals it even in the lowest. Shevet Dan, Adar and the stale-bread taunt of the mekalel and Haman show the claim that low Jews are discarded, refuted by the ever-fresh lechem hapanim. Purim is Hashem's love for the lowest Jew.

en: Purim is not a Jewish carnival; its holiness is greater than Yom Kippur.
Every sedra is the fabric of its week, and the first sedra of Adar contains the passuk of the lechem hapanim.
All Jewish souls are rooted in Knesses Yisrael, a level where they are one soul and no sin can enter.
In his innermost self every Jew wants to do Hashem's will; the yetzer hara only covers it, as the Rambam explains.
Even the lowest Jews, like Shevet Dan at the end of the camp, are rooted in 'reishis', and Haman's claim that they were cast off was false.
The lechem hapanim, which stayed fresh all week, shows that no Jew becomes stale before Hashem; it corresponds to Purim.
Purim is the day Hashem shows His love to every Jew, even the lowest, which is why the less observant are often the happiest on Purim.

title.en: Purim higher than Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets aside the regular shiur to speak about Purim, rejecting the view of it as a 'Jewish Halloween'. He brings the Chasam Sofer that the holiness of the Megillah is higher than Toras Moshe, and Rav Tzadok HaKohen that Purim is far greater than Yom Kippur.

title.en: The sedra shapes the week

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the weekly sedra is the fabric of the week. He tells of lumber merchants whose river stayed frozen because the children learned Miketz, and of the Ba'al HaTanya, who became the Maggid's ba'al korei because he knew the sedra's bond with each week, day and person called up.

title.en: Lechem hapanim and Knesses Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the passuk of the lechem hapanim in the first sedra of Adar. He brings the Noam Elimelech that there is a world called Knesses Yisrael where all Jewish souls are fused into one and no sin or accusation enters, and identifies it with the yechidah, the innermost level of the soul, where no Jew wants to sin.

title.en: Retzon Hashem, reishis, and Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Rambam on coercing a Jew until he says 'I want': inwardly every Jew wants Hashem's will. He brings the Maggid that the maamar of 'Bereishis' is above letters and thought, and that Jews are called 'reishis'. Yom Kippur reaches this root after ten days; Purim revealed it even when the Jews had sinned.

title.en: The lowest Jews: Dan, Adar and Haman

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the lowest souls are at the end of the Torah, like Shevet Dan, who were outside the clouds of glory and exposed to Amalek, and like the month of Adar. Haman thought he could prevail over these low Jews, but Hashem showed that every Jew is rooted in Bereishis; this is why Purim, kept in the second Adar next to Nisan, is greater than Yom Kippur.

title.en: The mekalel and the fresh lechem hapanim

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the son of the Egyptian man who was turned away from Shevet Dan and mocked the nine-day-old lechem hapanim, meaning that Hashem no longer cares for the lowest Jews. He answers that the lechem hapanim miraculously stayed fresh, so no Jew becomes stale before Hashem, and says Haman made the same claim; the Kabbalists say Haman was a gilgul of that man's father.

title.en: Memuchan, Purim as lechem hapanim, and matanos la'evyonim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the names of Achashverosh's ministers allude to the korbanos, with Memuchan alluding to the lechem hapanim, and that the shemen zayis corresponds to Chanukah and the lechem hapanim to Purim. Purim is the day Hashem shows His love to the lowest Jew, which is why the less observant are happiest on it. He closes with Purim wishes and explains that matanos la'evyonim reaches higher than ordinary tzedakah.

catalogTitle: ביאור אקדמות - מנהג ישראל' עיקר מהות של שבועות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the piyut Akdamus line by line, showing how the custom of saying it before the Shavuos Torah reading expresses the praise of Hashem, the song of the angels and the unique song of the Jewish people, and the reward awaiting them.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by stressing that although saying Akdamus is only a custom, a custom of the Jewish people carries the weight of Torah, and great tzaddikim were chosen to recite it. Following the piyut, he explains why one opens by asking permission, why the world is called olam (hidden), and why the fiftieth day is beyond counting. He describes the countless angels created anew each morning, each taking permission from the other, and draws a lesson of unity. The highest song, he says, is the silent one, and every Jew has his own point of knowledge of Hashem, hidden in his heart, illustrated by the story of the treasure under the bridge. Angels sing once in their lives; Jews may sing at every moment, in light and in darkness, like a soldier always on duty. He then explains toil in Torah, the nations' question 'what is your beloved', and the Jews' answer: the light of Moshiach, Olam Haba and the feast of the tzaddikim.

en: Saying Akdamus is only a custom, but a custom of the Jewish people carries the weight of Torah and of what was given at Sinai.
Every angel and every Jew is only one part of a great choir; each takes permission from the other, and only together does the song before Hashem become complete.
The highest song is the silent one: what a person cannot put into words, his private knowledge of Hashem according to his own measure.
The treasure of fear of Heaven lies in every Jew's heart; one need not leap to the heavens to find Hashem but only open the heart.
An angel may sing only once in its lifetime, while a Jew can sing to Hashem at every moment, morning and night, and in times of darkness as well.
Torah acquired through toil becomes a person's own, unlike Torah that came to him without effort.
The nations mock the Jews and invite them to assimilate; the Jews answer that in the days of Moshiach and in Olam Haba their greatness will be revealed.

title.en: Akdamus: a custom with the weight of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that saying Akdamus is not a Torah obligation but a custom, and that a custom of the Jewish people is Torah, as if given at Sinai. He describes the great holiness the tzaddikim saw in Akdamus and brings the Sefer Charedim that singing praise to Hashem is part of loving Him.

title.en: Asking permission and the hidden world

summary.en: Explaining the opening lines, the Mashgiach says one asks permission before speaking praise, as a chazzan must, and begins with only a few words. He explains that olam comes from 'hidden', that the fiftieth day is beyond counting, and that even if the heavens were parchment and the seas ink, Hashem's greatness could not be written.

title.en: The angels' song and the unity it teaches

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how Hashem created the worlds without effort, the countless angels created anew each morning, and the serafim who wait for permission and take it from one another. From this he teaches that every Jew must know he is one part of a great choir, and why the students of the Ba'al Shem Tov laid such weight on friendship.

title.en: The silent song and each Jew's own knowledge

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the angels' Kedushah with a roar like great waters, then explains the line about praise in a whisper: the highest song is the silent one, like the secrets of the Torah that cannot be conveyed to another. Every Jew knows Hashem according to his own measure, as in 'noda bashe'arim ba'alah', and has a root in Dovid HaMelech's Tehillim.

title.en: Where is His place? The treasure under the bridge

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out levels of praise, from the mouth to the lips to the innermost parts, as in 'Barchi nafshi'. He explains that one who has not yet arrived thinks Hashem is far away, but the Torah is 'not in heaven', and tells the story of the man who traveled to Hamburg for a treasure that lay under his own oven: the treasure of fear of Heaven is in every Jew's heart.

title.en: An angel sings once; a Jew every moment

summary.en: Explaining the lines on the angels' ordered Kedushah, the Mashgiach says a new angel may sing only once in its whole existence, while Hashem's beloved portion, Yisrael, praises Him at fixed times morning and evening. He asks why one should not use the chance the angels long for, to sing to Hashem at every moment.

title.en: A whole life as a song, morning and night

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that one comes to love of Hashem by contemplating His creation, and says this is most fitting at sunrise and sunset, when the whole creation sings. A person's whole life is a song, each with his own kind of niggun, and Yisrael praise Hashem in the morning and at night.

title.en: Serving in darkness: the soldier on duty

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that man was created with 'ratzo vashov', rising and falling, and that even the greatest tzaddikim had dark periods; then too one must serve Hashem. He tells of a soldier who left his post to swim and was caught by the king's inspection, and says a Jew is a soldier who must always be ready, in the morning and in the dark.

title.en: Toil in Torah and the crown of prayer

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem desires that Yisrael toil in Torah: Torah learned with toil is a person's own acquisition, unlike the Torah a child is taught before birth. When a Jew toils in Torah his prayer is accepted, and each accepted prayer becomes a jewel set in Hashem's crown, opposite His tefillin.

title.en: The Jews' mission and the waves of the nations

summary.en: Turning to Hashem's tefillin, the Mashgiach speaks of the greatness of Yisrael and their task to spread emunah among the nations, bringing the Rambam at the end of Hilchos Melachim. He then describes the nations coming at the Jews like waves crashing against grains of sand, asking why they sit in the beis medrash instead of joining their society.

title.en: 'What is your beloved?' and the Jews' answer

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that Akdamus here draws on the verse 'What is your beloved more than another, O fairest among women', and describes the nations' temptation to leave Yiddishkeit for honor and comfort. The Jews answer that the nations cannot yet understand, but when Moshiach comes the great light will show what Yisrael always had, even in exile.

title.en: The nations' shame and an endless joy

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when Moshiach comes the nations will admit that what they thought were great things were nothing, and Hashem will repay His enemies. He contrasts worldly pleasure, which ends once one is full, with the joy Hashem will give, which never becomes stale and is always renewed.

title.en: Olam Haba that no eye has seen

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that all the prophets prophesied only about the days of Moshiach, but of Olam Haba 'no eye has seen'. He explains with a rule that the holier a thing is, the more easily it is affected, and so Olam Haba is so holy that it was hidden even from the prophets.

title.en: The battle of the Shor HaBar and the Leviasan

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes, from the Midrashim, the great contest between the Shor HaBar and the Leviasan that the tzaddikim will see, and says only those who kept away from the nations' spectacles and sat over the Gemara will merit to watch it. He adds a hint that this contest reflects the struggle between the good and the evil inclination, which Hashem Himself will end.

title.en: The feast of the tzaddikim and the Torah reading

summary.en: The Mashgiach finishes the description of the great feast Hashem will prepare for the tzaddikim, with the wine that has been kept for them. He then turns to the congregation about to hear the Aseres HaDibros, as the tzaddikim heard them at Sinai, and blesses them to merit the company of the tzaddikim.

catalogTitle: מהר"ל - תורה היא מוכרח ולמעלה מן הזמן' קרבן שתי הלחם

oneLiner.en: Building on the Maharal, the Mashgiach explains that Matan Torah is above time, which is why the fiftieth day is not counted and why the Shavuos offering of the two loaves is chametz, and he describes the Sefirah work of 'kedoshim tihyu' that prepares a person for it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash on 'to everything there is a season': Adam's entry into and exit from Gan Eden, the Flood, and Avraham's milah all came at times fixed from Creation, since nothing in a world built with such harmony is chance. For Matan Torah, however, the verse says 'eis', not 'zman', because an 'eis' is a dimensionless point, and the Torah is above time. Therefore the fiftieth day is not counted, like Yovel and Yom Kippur. Following the Maharal, the Shavuos offering is chametz: chametz is the yetzer hara, and through the Torah it is refined and can serve Hashem. Sefirah refines the seven middos, counting downward from chesed because Shavuos brings Heaven down. The Mashgiach then develops 'kedoshim tihyu' as command and promise, with a story of the Rozvadover, a story of the Stoliner Rebbe's chesed, and practical guidance on growing in holiness step by step.

en: Every major event in history, including sins and their consequences, came at a time fixed in Hashem's plan from Creation; nothing happens by chance.
Matan Torah is called an 'eis', a point that has no extension, because the Torah is above time; for this reason the fiftieth day is not counted in Sefirah.
The Shavuos offering of the two loaves is chametz because through the Torah the yetzer hara, symbolized by chametz, is refined and can be used to serve Hashem.
Sefirah is the work of refining the seven middos, and it counts from chesed down to malchus because Shavuos is about bringing Heaven down to the world.
'Kedoshim tihyu' is both a command and a promise: if a person sanctifies himself a little, Hashem, who is holy, sanctifies him much more.
On Pesach the Jews were lifted up from Above with a strong hand, but the next day it is lost, and through Sefirah a person must reach Shavuos through his own work.
Holiness is built gradually: a person needs some gratification, and should give up a little at a time rather than all at once.

title.en: A set time for every great event

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash on 'to everything there is a season': Adam's entry into and exit from Gan Eden, the Flood, and Avraham's milah each had a fixed time. He explains from the harmony of creation that nothing is chance, and that even a sin and its consequence were prepared in advance.

title.en: 'Eis' and 'zman': the Torah above time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Midrash uses 'eis' for Matan Torah: 'zman' is a stretch of time, while 'eis' is a point with no dimension. Matan Torah is above time, like the fiftieth day beyond seven times seven, which is why it is not counted, and he compares it to Yovel and Yom Kippur.

title.en: Why the two loaves are chametz

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the two loaves of Shavuos are the only chametz offering, because chametz is the yetzer hara, and once the Torah comes into the world the yetzer hara can be refined and used for good. He brings 'I created the yetzer hara and created the Torah as its spice' and Moshe's answer to the angels.

title.en: Sefirah: counting down from chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Sefirah refines the seven middos, since man contains all the powers of creation, and asks why the count begins with chesed, the highest, rather than malchus. He answers from the Midrash that the Avos and Moshe brought the Shechinah down step by step: Shavuos is not climbing to Heaven but bringing Heaven down.

title.en: Matzah, chametz and the Shavuos meal

summary.en: Returning to the Maharal, the Mashgiach contrasts Pesach, when the Jews were lifted up and ate only matzah, with Shavuos, when Heaven comes down and the refined chametz is offered. He explains why all agree that Shavuos requires eating, and why the only communal shelamim come with the two loaves.

title.en: 'Kedoshim tihyu': command and promise

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that parshas Kedoshim falls in the Sefirah weeks because its theme is the work of becoming holy, and that 'kedoshim tihyu' is both a command and a promise. He brings Rashi and the Ramban, the significance of the third week, and the Gemara that for a tzaddik going beyond the letter of the law becomes his law.

title.en: The Rozvadover's three 'Ani Hashem'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Reb Moshe'le of Rozvadov, a grandson of the Ropshitzer, spoke on parshas Kedoshim before chassidim, simple people and mocking maskilim, applying each of the three 'Ani Hashem Elokeichem' to one group. He concludes that every person has a connection to Hashem according to his level.

title.en: From the Seder's gift to one's own work

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that 'kedoshim tihyu' is the theme running through Sefirah, rising each day to a higher holiness. On Pesach night Hashem lifted the Jews with a strong hand, but the next morning it is lost and the work begins, and he reads 'when your son asks you tomorrow' as the question of the morning after the Seder.

title.en: Using the middah of chesed for good

summary.en: The Mashgiach says man was created to sanctify himself through his own work, beginning with the middah of chesed, which must be used to love Hashem, Jews, tzaddikim and the Torah. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'chesed hu', and teaches that one's love of Hashem is measured by one's love of a fellow Jew.

title.en: The Stoliner Rebbe's chesed; help from Above

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of the Stoliner Rebbe in Williamsburg, a man of boundless chesed who hosted simple and far-off people, including a taxi driver at the Pesach Seder. He then explains the Midrash that opens Kedoshim with 'may He send your help from the Sanctuary': a person cannot sanctify himself alone, and Hashem helps.

title.en: Gratification and growing step by step

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a person needs some gratification, and that suddenly cutting off all pleasures leads to breakdown; one gives up a little at a time until one no longer needs it. He describes Jews whose pleasure is Torah and davening, and tells of Reb Nachum of Chernobyl, who his friends said grew stout from Torah.

catalogTitle: ז' שבועות של ספירה = ז' שמיטות ויובל; ביאור ענין יבום - חזרה לשורש

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven weeks of Sefirah are like seven shemitos leading to yovel, the time when every Jewish soul returns to its root, and that yibum, Megillas Rus and even the berachah over bread are part of this same return.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the seven weeks of Sefirah as seven shemitos, with Shavuos as yovel, when every Jew returns to his inheritance. Moshe counted every soul, including future gilgulim, and a soul that did not complete its part of the Torah returns, as Megillas Rus shows: Machlon was brought back through Boaz's yibum and Oved, the root of Beis Dovid. Since the yeshivah is learning Yevamos, he explains its inner meaning through the Ramban on yibum and gilgul, and shows how Hashem guarded malchus Beis Dovid at every step. Through Rav Ashi's dream of Menashe, who taught where to break bread, he explains that Hashem fixes the 'first-baked part' first, and that hamotzi frees a soul's spark from the bread. He tells the Belzer Rav's story of the wheat, urges careful berachos and eating, and closes with the days of Sefirah as a tikkun leading to Matan Torah.

en: The seven weeks of Sefirah correspond to seven shemitos, and Shavuos is like yovel and Yom Kippur, the time when every Jew returns to his root.
Every Jew is a letter of the Torah; a soul that left the world without completing its mission returns through gilgul or yibum so that the Torah stays whole.
Megillas Rus is read on Shavuos because it is the story of yibum: Machlon's soul returned through Boaz and Rus as Oved, from whom came malchus Beis Dovid.
Masechta Yevamos is hard because learning it brings tikkun to souls cut off from their root, and whatever brings such tikkun meets obstacles.
Hashem fixes malchus Beis Dovid first, like the part of the bread that is baked first, and so He accepted Menashe's teshuvah against the middas hadin.
Food holds sparks of souls, and a berachah said with attention brings them their tikkun; therefore eating is a great responsibility.

title.en: Seven weeks as seven shemitos and yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the seven weeks of Sefirah are seven shemitos and Shavuos is yovel, one with Yom Kippur, and that it is a time of freedom when every Jew returns to his inheritance.

title.en: Counted by Moshe; every Jew a letter of Torah

summary.en: Moshe counted all souls including future gilgulim; every Jew is a letter of the Torah, and one who did not complete his mission returns. The Mashgiach brings Megillas Rus: Machlon and Kilyon were earlier souls returning, and Machlon came back as Oved.

title.en: Return to the root; the cut branches of Shavuos

summary.en: Yom Kippur and Shavuos are times of return to the root, the Kisei Hakavod. The Mashgiach explains the custom of bringing trees in for Shavuos: the cut branches wilt, and one davens for Jewish souls cut off from their root.

title.en: Each Jew's nachalah and his share of Torah

summary.en: Each Jew's portion in Eretz Yisrael is his letter in the Torah and the source of his chiddushim. So Boaz, owner of the land, revealed the heter of a Moabite woman, while the closer relative, with no connection to it, refused Rus.

title.en: Why Masechta Yevamos is so hard

summary.en: Learning Yevamos deals with the tikkun of souls. Fixing oneself is hard and meets opposition, and what comes hard is a sign of one's mission; so too Yevamos is hard because, unknown to the learner, it brings tikkun to cut-off souls.

title.en: "Your wonders and thoughts are for us"

summary.en: From the Gemara in Yevamos about Dovid and Rechavam, the Mashgiach shows how Hashem guarded malchus Beis Dovid through every danger: Yehudah and Tamar, Boaz and Rus, and the Satan's claim, as with Esav, to a share of the holy soul.

title.en: Rus from Moav and the soul of Moshiach

summary.en: Rus came from Balak, who wanted to curse Israel, yet through Boaz came the blessing with Hashem's Name. Her soul was a branch cut off in Moav; Naomi, the Shechinah, went to gather it, beginning kibbutz galuyos with the soul of Moshiach himself.

title.en: The Ramban: yibum as the secret of gilgul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban in Vayeshev that yibum is a great secret, meaning gilgul, and that his commentary on Iyov answers the suffering of the righteous through earlier lives. Rabbeinu Bachya states it openly; the closest relative can best bring the soul back.

title.en: Boaz, "a son to Naomi", and helping another Jew

summary.en: Continuing the Ramban, the Mashgiach explains that Boaz as closest relative could bring back Machlon, so the neighbors called Oved 'a son to Naomi'. He adds that every help to another Jew, learning with him or even answering amen, is a kind of yibum.

title.en: Dipping bread in vinegar: Menashe

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Shabbos that Boaz hinted to Rus about six tzaddikim, and that 'dip your bread in vinegar' meant Menashe. He asks why Boaz needed to tell her this, and introduces the Gemara in Sanhedrin about Rav Ashi and Menashe.

title.en: Menashe teaches where to break bread

summary.en: Menashe appears to Rav Ashi in a dream and teaches that one breaks bread where it is baked first. The Mashgiach concludes that Menashe became the teacher of all Israel for hamotzi, and this was Boaz's comfort to Rus: even the 'vinegar' would become a rav.

title.en: The tunnel under the Kisei Hakavod

summary.en: Menashe did teshuvah in captivity, and the Gemara says Hashem dug a tunnel under the Kisei Hakavod so the middas hadin could not block it. The Mashgiach explains that Menashe carried the spark of Moshiach, and Hashem's original plan for creation stands above the middas hadin.

title.en: The Belzer Rav and the fallen kugel

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rebbe Shalom of Belz had a piece of kugel that fell to the floor picked up and eaten, and told the story of a grain of wheat that prayed at every stage to be eaten with a berachah.

title.en: Sparks in food and the eleven melachos of bread

summary.en: Every food holds sparks of souls brought by hashgachah pratis, and a proper berachah gives them tikkun. Bread passes through eleven melachos, matching eleven levels of klipah, until baking, its last tikkun.

title.en: The first-baked place: malchus Beis Dovid

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what Menashe knew that Rav Ashi did not, and answers that the part baked first is reaching its tikkun first by hashgachah. Malchus Beis Dovid, who must fix the world, is fixed first, like the Kohen Gadol who atones for himself first; hamotzi takes the spark out of the bread.

title.en: Eating as a battle: how to make hamotzi

summary.en: The ten words of hamotzi match the ten powers of the soul. Eating is a great responsibility, 'lechem' from 'milchamah'; the Mashgiach gives the parable of a relative pleading for attention and describes washing, cutting and dipping in salt with kavanah.

title.en: Boaz winnowing; Menashe's mother Chefzibah

summary.en: Boaz winnowed barley the night Rus came: of the three melachos of sorting, winnowing is done by the wind, by Hashem Himself, who refines malchus Beis Dovid. Menashe's mother was Chefzibah, 'My desire is in her'; only grain of Eretz Yisrael passes through all eleven melachos and receives a berachah.

title.en: Sefirah's tikkun and the night of Shavuos

summary.en: The days of Sefirah are a tikkun of the soul toward Shavuos. The Mashgiach brings the Kozhnitzer Maggid that even the last day can repair all fifty, the Zera Kodesh on Shavuos night, and says that today each Jew who takes on Torah is a lone individual, beloved to Hashem.

catalogTitle: Peeking Under the Costume of פורים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Adar, the lowest and most hidden month, carries the Megillah's personal message that Hashem is near even to the lowest Jew, and that in a year of a second Adar Hashem Himself completes what is missing.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens the month of Adar by saying that Purim is widely misunderstood: its clowning and wine are an anesthetic for a remedy too strong to take awake. Purim has its own masechta, and Rav Masna opens the Megillah with the passuk that Hashem is near to us. Rashi calls the Megillah a letter, and the Mashgiach explains that a letter is addressed to one person: the Megillah speaks to each reader privately. He then describes the ladder of souls, places and times. Our generation is the heel, yet still bound to the head, as the fingernail was once in the embryo. Nisan, from nes, is the month of open miracles; Adar, from aderes, a cloak, is the month of hidden ones. Adar matches the tribe of Dan at the rear of the camp, whom Amalek attacked as rejected. The Megillah answers that Hashem forsakes no Jew. In a leap year Adar Sheni has no permutation of the Divine Name, and Hashem Himself is the added one, so Purim belongs to the lowest.

en: The Mashgiach says Purim's clowning and wine serve as an anesthetic for a spiritual remedy too strong to take with open eyes, and Purim works whether or not one feels it.
The key to the Megillah, from Rav Masna's opening passuk, is that Hashem is near to us even when events make Him seem far.
Because the Megillah is called a letter, its message is addressed privately to each Jew who reads it.
Nisan is the month of revealed miracles and Adar the month of hidden ones, yet Adar holds as many miracles as Nisan.
Amalek attacked Dan, the rejected tribe at the rear, and Parshas Zachor teaches that Hashem never forsakes even the lowest Jew.
In a year with a second Adar, the thirteenth month has no permutation of the Divine Name, and Hashem Himself is the 'kolel', the added one who completes Klal Yisrael.
